entities.name: Sibt ibn al-Jawzi
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Shams al-Din Abu al-Muzaffar Yusuf ibn Kizoghlu, famously known as Sibṭ ibn al-Jawzī (1185–1256 CE), was a preeminent Islamic scholar, historian, and preacher of the Ayyubid period, whose intellectual lineage traced directly to his renowned grandfather, the polymath Ibn al-Jawzī. Born in Baghdad, a vibrant intellectual hub still under the nominal authority of the Abbasid Caliphate, Sibṭ ibn al-Jawzī rose to prominence as a leading voice in Damascus, then a critical center of Sunni scholarship and political power under Ayyubid rule. His extensive body of work, particularly his monumental universal history, *Mir'at al-Zaman fi Tarikh al-A'yan* (Mirror of the Times concerning the Notables), provides an invaluable lens into the political, social, and intellectual currents of the 12th and 13th centuries across the Islamic world, a period marked by both internal strife and the external pressures of the Crusades and emerging Mongol threat.

Sibṭ ibn al-Jawzī's career spanned both scholarly pursuits and public life. He lectured extensively in Damascus, often attracting large audiences with his eloquent preaching, which blended historical narratives, legal discussions, and ethical exhortations. His *Mir'at al-Zaman*, a sprawling thirty-volume chronicle, meticulously documents events from creation to his own time, drawing upon a vast array of earlier sources, many of which are now lost. Beyond history, he penned works on *hadith* (prophetic traditions), *fiqh* (Islamic jurisprudence), Qur'anic exegesis (*tafsir*), and asceticism, demonstrating a broad command of the Islamic sciences. His intellectual independence was notable; he often critiqued established views and engaged in theological debates, reflecting a nuanced approach to religious thought within the Hanbali school, though he also embraced a broader ecumenical spirit.
